# DISA Kubernetes STIG: what kube-noob's rules judge, and what no manifest can show

<!-- Generated by scripts/stig_crosswalk.py. Do not edit: run the script. -->

Benchmark: **Kubernetes Security Technical Implementation Guide**, **Version 2, Release 6**, published 2026-02-12, **92 rules** (18 CAT I, 74 CAT II, 0 CAT III). NIST's National Checklist Program lists it at [ncp.nist.gov/checklist/revision/6655](https://ncp.nist.gov/checklist/revision/6655).

**This page is not a STIG assessment and not an ATO artifact.** It says which of DISA's checks a kube-noob rule reads, and nothing about any cluster. kube-noob reads the manifests it is given; a STIG is assessed against a running system by a person who signs for the result. A finding from a mapped rule is evidence an assessor can use, and a clean run of a mapped rule is not a `Not a Finding`. Every row marked `not determinable from manifests` needs cluster or node evidence, which the row names, and kube-noob has no opinion on it at all. Nothing here is a statement by or on behalf of DISA.

**A managed control plane has no static pod manifest to give.** On EKS, AKS, GKE and ROSA with hosted control planes the API server, controller manager, scheduler and etcd run outside the cluster, so every row that reads a control plane static pod manifest is not determinable there, whatever its status says below: the status describes the rule, and the rule has nothing to read. KN-S038 and KN-S039 decline when no kube-apiserver or etcd container is in the input, and a declined rule is never counted as clean. The same holds for an application bundle audited on its own. On OpenShift, where operators write the control plane's arguments, KN-S038 declines a kube-apiserver manifest with that reason, and this STIG is not the one that applies.

## Where the rule list came from

The authoritative source is DISA's XCCDF. Neither ncp.nist.gov nor public.cyber.mil could be read when the list was pinned (2026-11-28), so the ids, rule ids, severities and titles were parsed from MITRE SAF's two InSpec profiles for this release, which carry DISA's metadata as tags: [cluster](https://github.com/mitre/k8s-cluster-stig-baseline/tree/e88e074e5732b6fd74f1a81cab62b45f237b61cd/controls) and [node](https://github.com/mitre/k8s-node-stig-baseline/tree/be9be05bb2f402f099c40e6803b7fa2de0291b74/controls). The sha256 over the control files parsed is `b2524d154e5a3f9aa017248d5274b4bbc5d72d1b59bc3044464885dd4301f5c1`. Every id, rule id and severity was then compared with <https://cyber.trackr.live/api/stig/Kubernetes/2/6> and <https://www.stigviewer.com/stigs/kubernetes>, which agreed on all 92. The pinned list is `src/kube_noob/data/stig/kubernetes-stig.yaml`; its sha256 is `e1658a307e225ca8b1e0c153bdba0ed3d3ed0407dd583162c07700fe312f6e7d`, recomputed by `scripts/stig_crosswalk.py --check` and `tests/test_stig_crosswalk.py`. It carries DISA's rule titles and one line per check in kube-noob's own words; DISA's check, fix and discussion text is not reproduced here. Read the rule itself before you rely on a row.

## Counts

No status on this page is a pass. `covered` says a rule reads what the check reads; whether a cluster meets the check is a different question, answered by running the rule on that cluster's manifests and then by an assessor.

| Status | CAT I | CAT II | CAT III | All |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| covered | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 |
| partly | 1 | 6 | 0 | 7 |
| not determinable from manifests | 5 | 35 | 0 | 40 |
| not covered | 11 | 32 | 0 | 43 |
| **All** | 18 | 74 | 0 | 92 |

- `covered`: a kube-noob rule judges this check from a manifest. The row says how, and where the rule is stricter.
- `partly`: a rule judges part of the check. The row names the part it does not judge.
- `not determinable from manifests`: the check reads something no manifest holds. The row names the evidence it needs.
- `not covered`: a manifest could decide it, and no kube-noob rule reads it yet. These rows are the rule backlog.

9 of the 92 rules have a kube-noob rule behind them, through 7 rules: `KN-S011`, `KN-S013`, `KN-S015`, `KN-S017`, `KN-S026`, `KN-S038`, `KN-S039`.

What each check reads decides most of this, so here it is by source:

| The check reads | Rules | covered | partly | not determinable from manifests | not covered |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| control plane static pod manifest | 43 | 2 | 4 | 0 | 37 |
| kubelet process and configuration file | 10 | 0 | 0 | 10 | 0 |
| file ownership and mode on a node | 22 | 0 | 0 | 22 | 0 |
| node or cluster state | 4 | 0 | 0 | 4 | 0 |
| objects in the cluster | 9 | 0 | 3 | 0 | 6 |
| PPSM list and system documentation | 4 | 0 | 0 | 4 | 0 |

## The 9 rules a kube-noob rule judges

Each of these is run on a fixture by `tests/test_stig_crosswalk.py`: the manifest the rule reports, the one it does not, and for a `partly` row the manifest that is a finding to DISA and clean to kube-noob.

### V-242379 — The Kubernetes etcd must use TLS to protect the confidentiality of sensitive data during electronic dissemination. (CAT II, partly)

- **The check:** The etcd static pod manifest: a finding when `--auto-tls` is absent or true.
- **Judged:** `--auto-tls=true` with no `--cert-file` or `--key-file`, on an etcd whose client side listens with TLS on a network address: etcd then serves a self-signed certificate and accepts any client.
- **Not judged:** An absent `--auto-tls` (etcd's default is false, and KN-S039 reads the default as off, where this check wants the flag written), `--auto-tls=true` beside a certificate pair (etcd ignores the switch, the check does not), and an etcd that listens on loopback only.
- **Rules:** `KN-S039` (etcd serves clients or peers in plaintext, or without client certificates)

### V-242380 — The Kubernetes etcd must use TLS to protect the confidentiality of sensitive data during electronic dissemination. (CAT II, partly)

- **The check:** The etcd static pod manifest: a finding when `--peer-auto-tls` is absent or true.
- **Judged:** `--peer-auto-tls=true` with no `--peer-cert-file` or `--peer-key-file`, on an etcd whose peer side listens with TLS on a network address.
- **Not judged:** An absent `--peer-auto-tls` (the default is false, and this check wants the flag written), `--peer-auto-tls=true` beside a peer certificate pair, and an etcd whose peer listener is loopback only.
- **Rules:** `KN-S039` (etcd serves clients or peers in plaintext, or without client certificates)

### V-242382 — The Kubernetes API Server must enable Node,RBAC as the authorization mode. (CAT II, covered)

- **The check:** The kube-apiserver static pod manifest: a finding when `--authorization-mode` is absent or names AlwaysAllow.
- **Judged:** An absent or empty `--authorization-mode` with no `--authorization-config` (the upstream default is AlwaysAllow), and AlwaysAllow anywhere in the list. An `--authorization-config` file, ABAC and Webhook are declined with the reason, never passed.
- **Note:** The check text asks only that AlwaysAllow is not in effect; the rule title's Node,RBAC is not what it tests, and KN-S038 does not require Node either.
- **Rules:** `KN-S038` (kube-apiserver allows anonymous requests or authorizes every request)

### V-242390 — The Kubernetes API server must have anonymous authentication disabled. (CAT I, covered)

- **The check:** The kube-apiserver static pod manifest: a finding when `--anonymous-auth` is true.
- **Judged:** `--anonymous-auth=true`. KN-S038 is stricter than the check: it also reports an absent flag, because the upstream default is true. An `--authentication-config` file with no `--anonymous-auth` is declined, never passed.
- **Note:** Where AlwaysAllow is also in effect KN-S038 reports that once, as the authorization finding, and does not repeat anonymous access in a second one: the rule fires either way.
- **Rules:** `KN-S038` (kube-apiserver allows anonymous requests or authorizes every request)

### V-242414 — The Kubernetes cluster must use non-privileged host ports for user pods. (CAT II, partly)

- **The check:** Pods in user namespaces: a finding when one uses a privileged host port.
- **Judged:** Every `hostPort` a container declares, with the port number in the finding.
- **Not judged:** Which of them the check counts. KN-S011 reports a `hostPort` of 1024 and above and one in `kube-system` the same as a privileged one in a user namespace, so a KN-S011 finding is not by itself a finding here: read the port and the namespace. A `hostNetwork` pod that binds a privileged port without declaring `hostPort` is KN-S009's finding, not this rule's.
- **Rules:** `KN-S011` (hostPort used)

### V-242423 — Kubernetes etcd must enable client authentication to secure service. (CAT II, partly)

- **The check:** The etcd static pod manifest: a finding when `--client-cert-auth` is absent or false.
- **Judged:** An absent or false `--client-cert-auth` with no `--trusted-ca-file`, on an etcd whose client side listens with TLS on a network address: any client that reaches the port is accepted without a certificate.
- **Not judged:** An absent or false `--client-cert-auth` beside a `--trusted-ca-file` (etcd requires a client certificate then, so KN-S039 is clean, and this check is still a finding), and an etcd that listens on loopback only.
- **Rules:** `KN-S039` (etcd serves clients or peers in plaintext, or without client certificates)

### V-242426 — Kubernetes etcd must enable client authentication to secure service. (CAT II, partly)

- **The check:** The etcd static pod manifest: a finding when `--peer-client-cert-auth` is absent or false.
- **Judged:** An absent or false `--peer-client-cert-auth` with no `--peer-trusted-ca-file`, on an etcd whose peer side listens with TLS on a network address.
- **Not judged:** An absent or false `--peer-client-cert-auth` beside a `--peer-trusted-ca-file` (etcd requires a peer certificate then, so KN-S039 is clean, and this check is still a finding), and an etcd whose peer listener is loopback only.
- **Rules:** `KN-S039` (etcd serves clients or peers in plaintext, or without client certificates)

### V-274883 — Sensitive information must be stored using Kubernetes Secrets or an external Secret store provider. (CAT I, partly)

- **The check:** Every workload and ConfigMap in the cluster, read by a person: a finding when one holds sensitive information outside a Secret.
- **Judged:** A credential kube-noob recognises by name or by shape: a literal value in a credential-named `env` variable or a credential passed in `command` or `args` (KN-S013), and a credential-named key, a URL with a password, a private key or a token in a ConfigMap (KN-S026).
- **Not judged:** Sensitive information that is not a credential, or does not look like one: a personal identifier, a customer record, an internal hostname. The check is a manual review against what the organisation calls sensitive, and no pattern stands in for that.
- **Rules:** `KN-S013` (Secret value hard-coded in environment); `KN-S026` (Credential stored in a ConfigMap)

### V-274884 — Kubernetes must limit Secret access on a need-to-know basis. (CAT II, partly)

- **The check:** RBAC and workloads: a finding when an account can read Secrets, or a workload mounts one, without a documented requirement.
- **Judged:** Which roles can read Secrets: `list` or `watch` on Secrets, and `get` on Secrets with no `resourceNames` (KN-S017), and a wildcard in `resources` or `verbs`, which includes them (KN-S015).
- **Not judged:** Whether a requirement is documented, which is the whole of the finding. KN-S017 also treats `get` limited to named Secrets as least privilege and says nothing, where this check still wants the requirement on paper; and no rule lists which workloads mount which Secret.
- **Rules:** `KN-S015` (RBAC wildcard grants); `KN-S017` (RBAC privilege-escalation paths)
